questions.text: Bamboo is technically a grass, yet some species can grow almost a metre in a single day. Because it regenerates from its roots after harvesting, architects increasingly treat it as a renewable alternative to timber. Its weakness has always been durability: untreated, it rots and attracts insects, so modern construction depends on careful drying and chemical protection.

zh.Bamboo is technically a grass, yet some: 竹子在學術上屬於禾草類植物，但有些品種一天之內就能長高將近一公尺。由於採收後竹子能從根部再生，建築師越來越把它視為木材的可再生替代品。它一直以來的弱點是耐久性：未經處理的竹子會腐爛並招來蟲害，因此現代營建工程仰賴細心的乾燥處理與化學防護。

questions.text: Double-entry bookkeeping, formalised by an Italian friar in the fifteenth century, records every transaction twice, once as a debit and once as a credit. The elegance of the system lies in its built-in check: if the two columns fail to balance, an error has been made somewhere. Five centuries later, the same principle still underpins global finance.

zh.Double-entry bookkeeping, formalised by: 複式簿記由一位義大利修士在十五世紀加以系統化，它把每一筆交易記錄兩次：一次記為借方，一次記為貸方。這個制度的精妙之處在於它內建的檢核機制：如果兩欄數字不平衡，就代表某處出了錯。五個世紀後，同樣的原則仍然支撐著全球金融體系。

questions.text: The human gut contains trillions of bacteria, and their combined genetic material outnumbers our own by a wide margin. Researchers once dismissed these microbes as passengers, but they now appear to influence digestion, immunity and even mood. What remains unclear is how much of this relationship we can deliberately change through diet.

zh.The human gut contains trillions of bact: 人類的腸道中有數兆個細菌，它們的遺傳物質總量遠遠超過我們自身的遺傳物質。研究人員過去把這些微生物視為無關緊要的「乘客」，但現在看來，它們會影響消化、免疫力，甚至情緒。目前仍不清楚的是，我們能在多大程度上透過飲食刻意改變這種關係。

questions.text: Volcanic eruptions can cool the planet as well as heat it. When a large eruption injects sulphur high into the atmosphere, the resulting particles reflect sunlight back into space. After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, average global temperatures fell by roughly half a degree for more than a year.

zh.Volcanic eruptions can cool the planet a: 火山爆發既能使地球升溫，也能使地球降溫。當一次大規模噴發把硫注入高層大氣時，所形成的微粒會把陽光反射回太空。1991 年皮納圖博火山爆發後，全球平均氣溫下降了大約半度，持續超過一年。

questions.text: Most people assume that memory works like a recording, faithfully storing events for later playback. In reality, each time we recall an experience we partly rebuild it, filling gaps with expectation and later knowledge. This is why confident eyewitnesses can be sincerely, and sometimes disastrously, wrong.

zh.Most people assume that memory works lik: 大多數人以為記憶就像錄影一樣，忠實地儲存事件以便日後重播。事實上，我們每次回想一段經歷時，都會部分地重建它，用預期和後來得知的資訊來填補空白。這就是為什麼充滿自信的目擊證人，可能真誠地犯錯，而且有時錯得造成災難性的後果。

questions.text: Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over the past decade, with hives appearing on office roofs and hotel terraces. Cities can be surprisingly good habitats, offering a long flowering season and fewer pesticides than intensive farmland. However, ecologists warn that too many honeybees may compete with the wild pollinators that depend on the same flowers.

zh.Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over: 過去十年來，都市養蜂迅速發展，蜂箱出現在辦公大樓屋頂和飯店露台上。城市可以是出乎意料的良好棲地，花季長，農藥也比集約化農地少。然而，生態學家警告，蜜蜂過多可能會與依賴同樣花朵的野生授粉昆蟲互相競爭。

questions.text: The printing press did not simply make books cheaper; it changed what counted as knowledge. Once identical copies could circulate across Europe, scholars could compare the same page, spot errors and build on one another’s work. Standardised texts made disagreement more precise, and precision made progress faster.

zh.The printing press did not simply make b: 印刷機不只是讓書變得更便宜；它改變了什麼才算是知識。一旦完全相同的副本能在歐洲各地流通，學者就能比對同一頁內容、找出錯誤，並在彼此的研究基礎上繼續發展。標準化的文本讓分歧變得更精確，而精確則讓進步變得更快。

questions.text: Desalination plants turn seawater into drinking water by forcing it through membranes fine enough to trap salt. The technology is reliable but energy hungry, and the concentrated brine left behind must be returned to the sea without harming marine life. For dry coastal cities, it is often an expensive insurance policy against drought.

zh.Desalination plants turn seawater into d: 海水淡化廠把海水加壓推過細密到足以攔住鹽分的薄膜，將它轉化為飲用水。這項技術可靠但耗能很高，而且留下的高濃度鹵水必須排回海中，同時不能傷害海洋生物。對乾燥的沿海城市來說，它往往是一份用來對抗乾旱的昂貴保險。

questions.text: Sleep patterns change markedly during adolescence. Teenagers’ internal clocks shift later by up to two hours, making it genuinely difficult for them to fall asleep early. Several school districts that moved their first lessons to a later start have reported better attendance, improved grades and fewer car accidents among young drivers.

zh.Sleep patterns change markedly during ad: 青春期的睡眠模式會明顯改變。青少年的生理時鐘會往後延遲多達兩小時，使他們真的很難早早入睡。幾個把第一堂課延後開始的學區表示，學生的出席率提高、成績進步，年輕駕駛發生的車禍也減少了。

questions.text: Glass is often described as a slow-moving liquid, a claim supported by the observation that old church windows are thicker at the bottom. The explanation is less exotic. Medieval glassmakers could not produce panes of even thickness, and builders usually installed the heavier edge at the base, where it was more stable.

zh.Glass is often described as a slow-movin: 玻璃常被形容為一種流動緩慢的液體，支持這個說法的觀察是：老教堂的窗戶底部比較厚。但真正的解釋並沒有那麼玄妙。中世紀的玻璃工匠無法製造出厚度均勻的玻璃板，而建築工人通常會把較重的一邊裝在底部，因為那樣比較穩固。

questions.text: Before refrigeration, salt was one of the most valuable goods in the world, because it allowed meat and fish to be preserved for months. Entire trade routes were organised around it, and several European cities grew wealthy by controlling its supply. Even the word salary is thought to be connected to payments made in salt.

zh.Before refrigeration, salt was one of th: 在冷藏技術出現之前，鹽是世界上最有價值的商品之一，因為它能讓肉類和魚類保存好幾個月。整條貿易路線都圍繞著鹽而建立，好幾個歐洲城市也因為掌控鹽的供應而致富。就連 salary（薪水）這個字，一般也認為與用鹽支付的報酬有關。

questions.text: Chameleons are famous for changing colour, but camouflage is not usually the main reason. Their skin contains layers of tiny crystals that reflect light differently as they are stretched or relaxed. Most dramatic changes occur during contests between males or during courtship, when a bright display communicates strength far more effectively than hiding would.

zh.Chameleons are famous for changing colou: 變色龍以會變色而聞名，但偽裝通常不是主要原因。牠們的皮膚含有好幾層微小的晶體，這些晶體在被拉伸或放鬆時，反射光線的方式會有所不同。最劇烈的顏色變化發生在雄性之間的競爭或求偶期間，此時鮮豔的展示比躲藏更能有效地傳達力量。

questions.text: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, which stretches the oceans into two bulges on opposite sides of the planet. As the Earth rotates through these bulges, most coastlines experience two high tides each day. The sun has a smaller effect, strengthening the tides when it lines up with the moon.

zh.Tides are caused mainly by the gravitati: 潮汐主要是由月球的引力造成的，它把海洋拉伸成位於地球兩側的兩個隆起。當地球自轉經過這兩個隆起時，大多數海岸每天都會出現兩次漲潮。太陽的影響較小，但當它與月球排成一直線時，就會使潮汐增強。

questions.text: The Library of Alexandria is often imagined as destroyed in a single catastrophic fire. Historians now think its decline was gradual, the result of reduced funding, political instability and scholars leaving for other cities over several centuries. The lesson is less dramatic but perhaps more relevant: institutions of knowledge usually fade through neglect.

zh.The Library of Alexandria is often imagi: 人們常想像亞歷山大圖書館是在一場災難性的大火中毀於一旦。歷史學家現在認為，它的衰落是漸進的，是經費減少、政治動盪，以及學者在幾個世紀間陸續前往其他城市所造成的結果。這個教訓沒那麼戲劇化，但或許更切合現實：知識機構通常是因為被忽視而逐漸凋零的。

questions.text: Open-plan offices were designed to encourage collaboration, but several studies suggest they have the opposite effect. When employees moved into open spaces, face-to-face interaction often fell, while email and messaging increased. Surrounded by noise and visibility, people appear to protect their concentration by withdrawing, putting on headphones and avoiding conversation altogether.

zh.Open-plan offices were designed to encou: 開放式辦公室的設計初衷是鼓勵合作，但好幾項研究顯示，它的效果正好相反。員工搬進開放空間後，面對面的互動往往減少了，而電子郵件和訊息則增加了。被噪音和他人的目光包圍時，人們似乎會以退縮的方式來保護自己的專注力，例如戴上耳機，並完全避免交談。

questions.text: European eels begin life in the Sargasso Sea, drift thousands of kilometres to the coasts of Europe, and spend decades in rivers before returning to spawn. Remarkably, no one has ever observed eels breeding in the wild. Much of what we know about their journey has been pieced together from larvae caught at sea.

zh.European eels begin life in the Sargasso: 歐洲鰻鱺在馬尾藻海出生，漂流數千公里到達歐洲沿岸，在河川中度過數十年，然後才返回產卵。值得注意的是，從來沒有人在野外觀察到鰻魚繁殖。我們對牠們旅程的大部分了解，都是從在海上捕獲的幼體拼湊出來的。

questions.text: A carbon tax works by making polluting activities more expensive, encouraging businesses and households to find cleaner alternatives. Economists generally prefer it to detailed regulation because it lets people decide where emissions can be cut most cheaply. The political difficulty is that the costs are visible immediately, while the benefits arrive slowly.

zh.A carbon tax works by making polluting a: 碳稅的運作方式是讓污染活動的成本變高，促使企業和家庭尋找更乾淨的替代方案。經濟學家通常比較偏好碳稅而不是詳細的法規，因為它讓人們自行決定在哪裡減排成本最低。政治上的困難在於，成本馬上就看得到，而好處卻來得很慢。

questions.text: For years, researchers claimed that speaking two languages strengthened general mental control, since bilingual people constantly suppress one language while using the other. Larger and more carefully designed studies have since struggled to reproduce this advantage. Learning a language clearly has many benefits, but a sharper mind in unrelated tasks may not be one of them.

zh.For years, researchers claimed that spea: 多年來，研究人員一直聲稱說兩種語言能增強整體的心智控制力，因為雙語者在使用一種語言時，必須不斷壓抑另一種語言。但後來規模更大、設計更嚴謹的研究，都難以重現這種優勢。學習語言顯然有許多好處，但在不相關的任務上頭腦更靈活，可能並不是其中之一。

questions.text: Roman harbour walls built two thousand years ago are still standing in seawater that would destroy modern concrete within decades. Analysis has shown that the Romans mixed volcanic ash with lime, and that seawater slowly triggered the growth of new minerals inside the structure. In effect, the material became stronger with age.

zh.Roman harbour walls built two thousand y: 兩千年前建造的羅馬港口牆，至今仍矗立在海水中，而同樣的海水會在數十年內摧毀現代混凝土。分析顯示，羅馬人把火山灰和石灰混合在一起，而海水會慢慢促使結構內部生成新的礦物。實際上，這種材料會隨著時間變得更加堅固。

questions.text: Roughly a third of the food produced worldwide is never eaten. In poorer countries, most of the loss happens early, because of poor storage and transport. In wealthier countries, it happens at the end of the chain, in shops and homes, where food is thrown away simply because it looks imperfect or has passed a date label.

zh.Roughly a third of the food produced wor: 全世界生產的食物中，大約有三分之一從來沒有被吃掉。在較貧窮的國家，大部分的損失發生在早期階段，原因是儲存和運輸不良。在較富裕的國家，損失則發生在供應鏈的末端，也就是商店和家庭中，食物只因為外觀不完美或過了標示日期就被丟棄。

questions.text: The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by a French doctor who felt uncomfortable placing his ear directly on a young patient’s chest. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tube and found that he could hear the heart more clearly than ever before. His simple improvisation became the most recognisable symbol of medicine.

zh.The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by: 聽診器是在 1816 年由一位法國醫師發明的，他對於把耳朵直接貼在一位年輕病人的胸口上感到不自在。他把一張紙捲成一根管子，發現自己能比以往任何時候都更清楚地聽到心跳聲。他這個簡單的臨時發明，後來成為醫學最具代表性的象徵。

questions.text: Adding lanes to a congested road rarely reduces traffic for long. The extra space makes driving more attractive, so people who previously travelled at other times, by other routes or by public transport begin to drive instead. Within a few years, the new road is often as crowded as the old one, a pattern known as induced demand.

zh.Adding lanes to a congested road rarely: 在壅塞的道路上增加車道，很少能長期減少交通量。多出來的空間讓開車變得更有吸引力，所以原本在其他時段出行、走其他路線或搭大眾運輸的人，都開始改為開車。不出幾年，新道路往往就和舊道路一樣擁擠，這種現象稱為「誘發需求」。

questions.text: During the last ice age, sea levels were more than a hundred metres lower than today, exposing land bridges between continents. One of these connected Asia and North America, allowing people and animals to cross on foot. When the ice melted, the bridge disappeared beneath the sea, separating populations that had once been connected.

zh.During the last ice age, sea levels were: 在上一次冰河時期，海平面比現在低了一百多公尺，露出了連接各大陸的陸橋。其中一座連接了亞洲和北美洲，讓人類和動物能夠徒步穿越。當冰融化後，這座陸橋就沉入海底，把原本相連的族群分隔開來。

questions.text: Microplastics have now been found almost everywhere scientists have looked, from Arctic snow to the deepest ocean trenches and even human blood. Their effects on health remain uncertain, largely because exposure is so widespread that it is difficult to find a comparison group that has not been exposed at all.

zh.Microplastics have now been found almost: 如今，科學家幾乎在所有調查過的地方都發現了塑膠微粒，從北極的雪到最深的海溝，甚至人類的血液中都有。它們對健康的影響仍不確定，主要是因為暴露的情況太普遍，很難找到一個完全沒有接觸過的對照組。

questions.text: Just-in-time manufacturing keeps very little stock, relying on parts arriving exactly when they are needed. The approach cuts storage costs and exposes inefficiencies, which is why it spread rapidly from Japanese carmakers to industries around the world. Its weakness became obvious during recent crises, when a single delayed component could halt an entire factory.

zh.Just-in-time manufacturing keeps very li: 及時生產制幾乎不保留庫存，而是仰賴零件在需要的時候準時送達。這種做法能降低倉儲成本並暴露出效率低落的環節，這也是它從日本汽車製造商迅速擴展到全世界各行各業的原因。它的弱點在最近幾次危機中變得十分明顯：只要一個零件延誤，就可能讓整座工廠停擺。

questions.text: Birds of the same species can sing noticeably different songs depending on where they live, much as human accents vary between regions. Young birds learn their songs by listening to adults nearby, so local variations are passed down through generations. In noisy cities, some species have even begun to sing at a higher pitch.

zh.Birds of the same species can sing notic: 同一種鳥會因為居住地不同而唱出明顯不同的歌，就像人類的口音會因地區而異。幼鳥是靠聆聽附近的成鳥來學唱歌的，所以地方性的差異會一代一代傳下去。在吵雜的城市裡，有些鳥類甚至開始用更高的音調唱歌。

questions.text: The wandering albatross can cross an ocean with barely a wingbeat. It rides the difference in wind speed between the wave troughs and the air above them, climbing and diving in a long spiral that costs almost nothing in energy. A bird may travel a thousand kilometres in a day and return to the same nest for decades.

zh.The wandering albatross can cross an oce: 漂泊信天翁幾乎不必拍動翅膀就能橫越整片海洋。牠利用波谷與其上空氣流速度的差異，沿著長長的螺旋路徑爬升又俯衝，幾乎不耗費任何能量。一隻鳥可能一天飛行一千公里，而且數十年都回到同一個巢。

questions.text: Saffron is the most expensive spice in the world because it must be picked by hand. Each crocus flower yields only three crimson threads, and it takes roughly a hundred and fifty thousand flowers to produce a single kilogram. The harvest lasts a few weeks and begins before dawn, while the flowers are still closed.

zh.Saffron is the most expensive spice in t: 番紅花是世界上最昂貴的香料，因為它必須靠人工採摘。每一朵番紅花只能取得三根深紅色的柱頭，要生產一公斤大約需要十五萬朵花。採收期只有短短幾週，而且要在天亮前、花朵還沒開放時就開始。

questions.text: The vacuum flask was invented for the laboratory, not the lunchbox. A Scottish chemist needed to keep liquefied gases cold and built a double-walled glass vessel with the air pumped out between the walls. Because heat cannot cross a vacuum by conduction, the contents held their temperature for hours. He never patented the design.

zh.The vacuum flask was invented for the la: 真空瓶最初是為實驗室而不是為午餐盒發明的。一位蘇格蘭化學家需要讓液化氣體保持低溫，於是做出一個雙層玻璃容器，並把兩層之間的空氣抽掉。由於熱無法以傳導方式穿過真空，瓶中的東西可以維持溫度好幾個小時。他從未為這個設計申請專利。

questions.text: Chopping an onion ruptures its cells, releasing an enzyme that converts a harmless compound into a volatile gas. The gas drifts upwards, dissolves in the film of moisture on the eye and forms a mild acid, which the eye flushes away with tears. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction considerably.

zh.Chopping an onion ruptures its cells, re: 切洋蔥會弄破它的細胞，釋放出一種酵素，把原本無害的化合物轉變成揮發性氣體。這種氣體往上飄散，溶解在眼睛表面的水膜中形成弱酸，而眼睛便以流淚把它沖走。先把洋蔥冷藏可以明顯減緩這個反應。

questions.text: Cork is harvested without felling a single tree. Every nine years the outer bark of a cork oak is cut away by hand, and the tree regrows it, continuing to do so for well over a century. Because the groves are left standing, they shelter rare birds and lynx that intensive farming would displace.

zh.Cork is harvested without felling a sing: 採收軟木不必砍倒任何一棵樹。每九年，人們會以手工割下栓皮櫟的外層樹皮，而樹木會再長出新的樹皮，並持續一個多世紀。由於這些樹林得以保留，它們庇護了稀有的鳥類與山貓，而集約農業會把這些動物趕走。

questions.text: Before the telegraph reached every town, armies and newspapers relied on pigeons. A trained bird could carry a message a hundred kilometres in two hours and find a loft it had not seen for months. Nobody is certain how they navigate, though the magnetic field and the position of the sun both seem to help.

zh.Before the telegraph reached every town,: 在電報普及到每個城鎮之前，軍隊和報社都依賴鴿子。一隻訓練有素的鴿子能在兩小時內把訊息送到一百公里外，並找到牠好幾個月沒見過的鴿舍。沒有人確定牠們如何導航，不過地磁場和太陽的位置似乎都有幫助。

questions.text: The Beaufort scale was written for sailors who had no instruments. Instead of numbers from a gauge, it describes what the sea and the sails are doing: ripples without crests at force one, and at force twelve a sea entirely white with driving spray. Two centuries later, forecasters still quote it.

zh.The Beaufort scale was written for sailo: 蒲福風級是為沒有儀器的水手而訂定的。它不以儀表上的數字為準，而是描述海面和船帆的狀態：一級時只有沒有浪峰的細波，到了十二級，海面則因強風吹起的水沫而一片雪白。兩個世紀之後，氣象預報員仍然引用它。

questions.text: Permafrost is ground that has stayed frozen for at least two years, and in parts of Siberia it runs more than a kilometre deep. It holds plant matter that never fully decayed, locking away roughly twice the carbon now in the atmosphere. As it thaws, that material rots and the gas escapes.

zh.Permafrost is ground that has stayed fro: 永凍土是至少連續兩年保持結凍的地層，在西伯利亞部分地區深達一公里以上。它封存著從未完全分解的植物殘骸，鎖住的碳大約是目前大氣中碳含量的兩倍。隨著它融化，這些物質開始腐爛，氣體便逸散出來。

questions.text: For most of the last century, every wildfire was put out as quickly as possible. The result was forests packed with dead wood, which burn far hotter when they finally catch. Fire services now set controlled burns in cool, damp weather, clearing the fuel before a summer fire can reach it.

zh.For most of the last century, every wild: 在上個世紀的大部分時間裡，每一場野火都被盡快撲滅。結果是森林裡堆滿枯木，一旦真的著火就燒得更猛烈。消防單位現在會在涼爽潮濕的天氣進行計畫性火燒，在夏季野火蔓延到之前先清除這些可燃物。

questions.text: The Suez Canal has no locks, because the Mediterranean and the Red Sea sit at almost the same level. What it does have is a narrow channel through soft sand, which must be dredged constantly. Roughly twelve per cent of world trade passes through a waterway barely wider than a city street.

zh.The Suez Canal has no locks, because the: 蘇伊士運河沒有船閘，因為地中海與紅海的水位幾乎相同。它真正的特點是一條穿過鬆軟沙地的狹窄航道，必須不斷疏浚。全球大約百分之十二的貿易，都通過這條寬度勉強超過一條城市街道的水道。

questions.text: When a school for deaf children opened in Nicaragua in the late 1970s, the pupils had no shared language. Within a few years they had built one themselves, with grammar their teachers had never taught. Linguists who arrived to study it found a rare thing: a language being born in real time.

zh.When a school for deaf children opened i: 一九七○年代末，尼加拉瓜成立了一所聾人兒童學校，當時學生之間沒有共同的語言。短短幾年內，他們自己創造出一套語言，還帶有老師從未教過的文法。前來研究的語言學家見到了罕見的現象：一種語言正在實時誕生。

questions.text: Lost-wax casting has barely changed in five thousand years. A model is shaped in wax, coated in clay and then heated, so the wax runs out and leaves a hollow mould behind. Molten metal is poured in, the clay is broken away, and what remains is a copy of the original.

zh.Lost-wax casting has barely changed in f: 失蠟鑄造法在五千年間幾乎沒有改變。先用蠟塑出模型，外面裹上黏土後加熱，蠟流出來，留下中空的模子。接著倒入熔融的金屬，敲掉黏土，剩下的就是原模型的複製品。

questions.text: In the 1630s a single tulip bulb could change hands for the price of a canal house in Amsterdam. Buyers were not gardeners but traders, selling contracts for bulbs still in the ground. When confidence broke in February 1637, prices collapsed within days and the contracts became worthless.

zh.In the 1630s a single tulip bulb could c: 在一六三○年代，一顆鬱金香球莖的成交價可以相當於阿姆斯特丹一棟運河旁的房子。買家並不是園丁，而是交易者，他們買賣的是還埋在土裡的球莖契約。一六三七年二月信心崩潰時，價格在幾天之內暴跌，那些契約也變得一文不值。

questions.text: Antarctica is governed by a treaty rather than by any country. Signed in 1959, it sets the whole continent aside for peaceful science, bans military activity and freezes every territorial claim without settling any of them. More than fifty states have now signed, and the agreement has held through decades of tension elsewhere.

zh.Antarctica is governed by a treaty rathe: 南極洲是由一項條約而不是任何國家所治理。這項條約於一九五九年簽署，把整個大陸保留給和平的科學研究，禁止軍事活動，並凍結所有領土主張，卻不解決其中任何一項。如今已有五十多個國家簽署，而在其他地區數十年的緊張局勢中，這項協議始終維持不墜。

questions.text: Sand is the most mined material on earth after water, and the world is running short of the kind that is useful. Desert sand is too round and smooth to bind in concrete, so builders take theirs from riverbeds and coasts, where the digging erodes banks and removes the habitat of fish.

zh.Sand is the most mined material on earth: 沙是地球上僅次於水、開採量最大的物料，而世界正逐漸缺乏可用的那種沙。沙漠裡的沙顆粒太圓滑，無法在混凝土中彼此咬合，所以建築業者從河床和海岸取沙，而這樣的開挖會侵蝕河岸並摧毀魚類的棲地。

questions.text: Night trains were written off as a relic of the age before cheap flights, yet several European routes have reopened. A sleeper leaves after dinner and arrives in time for a morning meeting, with no airport and no hotel bill. The carriages are expensive to run, so most new services depend on public support.

zh.Night trains were written off as a relic: 夜車曾被視為廉價航空出現之前的遺物，然而歐洲有好幾條路線已經重新開通。臥鋪列車在晚餐後出發，趕得上隔天早上的會議，既不必進機場，也省下旅館費用。這些車廂的營運成本很高，所以大多數新開的班次都仰賴公共補貼。

questions.text: There is no lead in a pencil. The grey core is graphite, a form of carbon whose atoms lie in sheets that slide over one another, which is why it leaves a mark on paper. Mixing the graphite with clay before firing controls the hardness, from a pale, scratchy line to a soft black one.

zh.There is no lead in a pencil. The grey c: 鉛筆裡並沒有鉛。那灰色的筆芯是石墨，一種碳的形式，它的原子排列成一層層的薄片，可以彼此滑動，這就是它能在紙上留下痕跡的原因。在燒製前把石墨與黏土混合可以控制硬度，從淡而刮紙的線條到柔軟的黑線都做得到。

questions.model: The line chart shows the percentage of adults owning a smartphone in two age groups between 2012 and 2024. Ownership rose in both groups throughout the period. Among 18 to 34 year olds it climbed from 66 per cent to 92 per cent by 2018 and then levelled off, reaching an almost universal 97 per cent. The over-55s started far lower, at just 18 per cent, but grew much faster, reaching 80 per cent by 2024. As a result, the gap between the two groups narrowed from 48 to 17 percentage points, suggesting that older adults are rapidly catching up.

Buildings and maintenance take the second largest portion at 16 per cent, followed by research equipment at 12 per cent and student services at 10 per cent. The smallest share, just 8 per cent, is spent on the library and IT. Overall, the chart shows that a university is mainly a people-based organisation, with most of its money spent on the staff who teach and run it.

questions.caption: Process diagram showing the five stages of recycling waste paper into new paper.
keys: the process has five stages
paper is first collected and sorted
it is mixed with water and broken down into pulp
ink, glue and other contaminants are removed
the pulp is pressed, dried and rolled into new paper, completing the cycle
questions.model: The diagram shows the five main stages in recycling waste paper. First, used paper is collected and sorted by type. It is then mixed with water and broken down into a soft pulp. In the third stage, ink, glue and other contaminants are removed so that the fibres are clean. After that, the pulp is pressed to squeeze out the water and then dried. Finally, the dried material is rolled into sheets of new paper, which can be sold and eventually recycled again. Overall, the process turns waste into a usable product through a clear sequence of cleaning and reshaping steps.

questions.model: The table lists the five largest coffee-producing countries. Brazil dominates, producing 66 million bags, which is 39 per cent of world output. Vietnam is a distant second with 29 million bags, or 17 per cent, so together these two countries produce more than half of the world’s coffee. The remaining three, Colombia, Indonesia and Ethiopia, each produce between 8 and 12 million bags, or 5 to 7 per cent. The table also shows the main type grown: Brazil, Colombia and Ethiopia mainly produce Arabica, while Vietnam and Indonesia focus on Robusta.

questions.caption: Process diagram showing five stages by which a proposal becomes law.
keys: the process has five stages
a draft bill is introduced and first debated in parliament
a committee examines it and may suggest amendments
it must be voted on in both houses
it becomes law after formal approval
questions.model: The diagram shows the five stages by which a proposal becomes law. First, a draft bill is introduced, and it is then debated for the first time in parliament. Next, it is sent to a committee, which examines the details and may suggest amendments. After that, the bill must be approved by a vote in both houses of parliament. Finally, it receives formal approval and becomes law. Overall, the process is designed to give a proposal several rounds of scrutiny before it can take effect.

zh.the process has five stages: 整個流程分為五個階段
zh.a draft bill is introduced and first deb: 草案被提出，並在議會中進行第一次辯論
zh.a committee examines it and may suggest: 由委員會審查，並可能提出修正
zh.it must be voted on in both houses: 必須在兩院中表決通過
zh.it becomes law after formal approval: 經過正式批准後成為法律
zh.The diagram shows the five stages by whi: 這張圖呈現一項提案成為法律的五個階段。首先，提出法案草案，接著在議會中進行第一次辯論。然後，草案被送交委員會，由委員會審查細節並可能提出修正。之後，法案必須在議會兩院表決通過。最後，它獲得正式批准，成為法律。整體而言，這個流程的設計是讓一項提案在生效之前經過好幾輪的審查。

questions.caption: Grouped bar chart of the percentage of men and women who exercise every week, in four age groups.
keys: weekly exercise declines with age for both men and women
young men exercise most, 68% compared with 61% of young women
the gap between men and women narrows with age
among people over 60, women exercise slightly more, 44% against 41%
overall participation falls from about two-thirds to just over 40%
questions.model: The bar chart shows the percentage of men and women who exercise every week in four age groups. For both sexes, exercise declines steadily with age. Among 18 to 29 year olds, men are clearly more active, at 68 per cent compared with 61 per cent of women. However, the gap narrows in older groups, and the figures are almost equal for those aged 45 to 59. Among people over 60, women are slightly more active, at 44 per cent against 41 per cent. Overall, weekly exercise falls from around two-thirds of young adults to just over forty per cent of older people.

questions.caption: Line chart of monthly visitors to a national park over one year, in thousands.
keys: visitor numbers peak in July at 84,000
January is the quietest month with 12,000
numbers rise steadily from March and sharply in early summer
August remains almost as busy as July, at 81,000
visits fall quickly after September back to winter levels
questions.model: The line chart shows the number of visitors to a national park each month over one year. In winter, numbers are low, with just 12,000 visitors in January. From March, visits rise steadily and then climb sharply in early summer, reaching a peak of 84,000 in July. August remains almost as busy, at 81,000. After that, numbers fall quickly, to 52,000 in September and just 13,000 by December. Overall, the park is highly seasonal, receiving around seven times as many visitors in midsummer as in midwinter.

questions.caption: Pie chart of the sources of a city’s electricity in 2024.
keys: natural gas is the largest single source, 38%
wind is second at 24%, followed by solar at 16%
renewables together (wind, solar, hydro) provide 48%, more than gas
nuclear supplies 14%

questions.model: The pie chart shows where a city obtained its electricity in 2024. Natural gas was the largest single source, providing 38 per cent. Wind came second with 24 per cent, followed by solar at 16 per cent and nuclear at 14 per cent, while hydroelectric power was the smallest source at 8 per cent. Although gas was the biggest individual source, the three renewable sources together, wind, solar and hydro, supplied 48 per cent of the city’s electricity, more than gas alone. Overall, the city relied on a fairly diverse mix of energy sources.

questions.caption: Process diagram of the water cycle in five stages.
keys: the water cycle is a continuous loop of five stages
water evaporates from the oceans
the vapour condenses into clouds
it falls as rain or snow
it collects in rivers and lakes and flows back to the sea
questions.model: The diagram illustrates the water cycle, a continuous process with five stages. First, heat from the sun causes water to evaporate from the oceans. As the water vapour rises and cools, it condenses to form clouds. The water then falls back to the ground as precipitation, in the form of rain or snow. After that, it collects in rivers and lakes, and finally it flows back to the sea, where the cycle begins again. Overall, the diagram shows how the same water moves endlessly between the oceans, the atmosphere and the land.

questions.caption: Process diagram of the six main stages in making chocolate.
keys: chocolate is made in six main stages
cocoa pods are harvested and the beans fermented
the beans are dried in the sun, then roasted and cracked
they are ground into a paste called cocoa liquor
this is mixed with other ingredients and moulded into bars
questions.model: The diagram shows the six main stages in making chocolate. First, cocoa pods are harvested and the beans are removed and left to ferment, which develops their flavour. The beans are then dried in the sun. Next, they are roasted and cracked open, and the inner parts are ground into a thick paste known as cocoa liquor. Finally, this is mixed with ingredients such as sugar and milk and poured into moulds to form bars. Overall, the process turns a raw agricultural crop into a finished product through a series of preparation and processing steps.

Germany is the lowest at 1,340 hours, which is about 780 hours, or roughly four months of a working week, below Mexico. Japan sits near the middle at 1,630, below Greece at 1,790. The three Asian countries shown are all under 20 hectares, so an average Australian farm is several hundred times the size of an average Bangladeshi one. questions.model: The grouped bar chart compares the share of sales made online in four retail categories in 2014 and 2024. Every category grew over the decade. Clothing roughly tripled from 11 to 34 per cent, and furniture grew almost fourfold from 7 to 26. Groceries remain the lowest by a wide margin, reaching only 14 per cent, which suggests that shoppers still prefer to choose fresh food in person.

questions.caption: Process diagram showing the six stages of treating river water to make it safe to drink.
keys: six stages from river to tap
debris is screened out first
a coagulant makes particles clump and settle
sand filtration then disinfection
treated water is stored before distribution
questions.model: The diagram shows the six stages by which river water is made safe to drink. First, screens remove leaves and other debris. The water then passes to a settling tank, where a coagulant makes fine particles clump together and sink. Next it filters down through beds of sand, which trap anything still suspended, before chlorine is added to kill bacteria. The treated water is held in a covered reservoir, which allows demand to be met at peak times, and is finally pumped through the mains to homes.

questions.text: Most of us think of a placebo as a trick: it only works if the patient believes they are receiving real medicine. A series of recent trials has challenged that assumption. In so-called open-label studies, patients with chronic back pain or irritable bowel syndrome were handed pills and told plainly that they contained no active ingredient. Remarkably, many still reported meaningful relief compared with patients who received no pills at all. Researchers think the ritual itself matters — taking something regularly, with the attention of a clinician, appears to trigger the body’s own pain-regulating systems. That does not mean placebos can cure disease; they have little effect on tumours or infections. But for conditions where symptoms are shaped by the brain’s interpretation of signals, honesty and effectiveness may not be in conflict after all.

Although placebos cannot cure diseases such as tumours or infections, the lecturer concluded that for symptom-driven conditions, honesty and effectiveness can coexist.

questions.text: The keyboard in front of you is a small lesson in economics. The QWERTY layout was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters, partly to reduce jamming when neighbouring keys were struck in quick succession. The mechanical problem disappeared generations ago, and several alternative layouts claim to be faster. Yet QWERTY has survived, and economists use it as a classic example of path dependence. Once millions of people have learned a system, and manufacturers, schools and employers have organised around it, the cost of switching becomes enormous, even if the alternative is better. Interestingly, later research has questioned how much faster the alternatives really are, which suggests a second lesson: when a standard has lasted this long, it is worth checking whether the story of its inferiority is itself exaggerated.

However, the speaker added that later research questions whether the alternatives are really faster, so claims that a standard is inferior may themselves be exaggerated.

questions.text: Scattered across parts of the deep ocean floor are potato-sized lumps called polymetallic nodules. They contain nickel, cobalt and manganese, the metals needed for electric vehicle batteries, and several companies are preparing to harvest them with robotic collectors. Supporters argue that mining the seabed could be less damaging than clearing rainforest for mines on land, and that the energy transition depends on these metals. Marine biologists are far more cautious. The nodules grow by only a few millimetres every million years, and they form the only hard surface on which many deep-sea species can live. Studies of test sites disturbed decades ago show that life has still not recovered. The central problem is that we are being asked to approve an industry in an ecosystem we have barely begun to describe.

questions.text: Over the last few years, hundreds of companies have trialled a four-day working week with no reduction in pay. The results have been more positive than many managers expected. In the largest trials, most firms reported that productivity held steady or even improved, while staff reported less burnout and fewer sick days. Recruitment also became easier, because the policy was attractive to job seekers. However, the picture is not uniform. The model works best in office jobs where output can be measured and meetings can be cut. In hospitals, schools and factories, where someone must be present for a fixed number of hours, a shorter week usually means hiring more staff. So the real question is not whether a four-day week works, but in which kinds of work it can pay for itself.

questions.text: Procrastination is often treated as a problem of time management, but psychologists increasingly see it as a problem of emotion regulation. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or insecure, delaying it provides immediate relief, even though we know it will cost us later. That short-term reward is why procrastination is so hard to break. Studies of students show that those who procrastinate most are not necessarily lazy or disorganised; they are often the ones most worried about failing. Interestingly, one of the most effective interventions is self-forgiveness. Students who forgave themselves for delaying revision before one exam procrastinated less before the next. The reasoning is that guilt adds another negative emotion to the task, making it even more tempting to avoid. So the solution is less about planners and more about how we treat ourselves when we fall behind.

Surprisingly, self-forgiveness helps: students who forgave themselves for delaying revision procrastinated less before the next exam, because guilt only adds another negative emotion. The lecturer concluded that the solution lies in how we treat ourselves.

questions.text: Almost every world map you have seen distorts the planet. It is impossible to flatten a sphere without stretching it somewhere, so every projection involves a compromise. The most famous, the Mercator projection, was designed in 1569 for sailors. Its great advantage is that a straight line on the map is a line of constant compass direction, which made navigation far simpler. The cost is size. Areas far from the equator are enormously enlarged, so Greenland appears roughly the size of Africa, when in reality Africa is about fourteen times larger. Because Mercator maps became the standard in classrooms, generations of students absorbed a distorted sense of the world. Cartographers now argue that the right projection depends on the purpose: Mercator for navigation, and equal-area projections when comparing the sizes of countries.

questions.text: Most of us hate waiting, but research on queues shows that how we feel about a wait depends less on its length than on how it is experienced. Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, which is why lifts have mirrors and theme parks entertain people in line. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, so a display saying fifteen minutes makes a wait more tolerable. Perhaps most importantly, unfair waits feel longer than fair ones. People become far more upset when someone who arrived later is served first. This is why a single queue feeding several counters, although not faster on average, is usually preferred to separate lines. For businesses, the lesson is that improving the experience of waiting can matter as much as reducing it.

questions.text: When we talk about coastal flooding, we usually focus on rising seas. But in many of the world’s largest coastal cities, the land itself is sinking, often faster than the sea is rising. The main cause is groundwater extraction. When water is pumped out of the layers of clay and sand beneath a city, those layers compact, and the surface drops. Parts of Jakarta have sunk by more than four metres over recent decades. The encouraging news is that subsidence can be slowed. Tokyo sank rapidly in the mid-twentieth century, but after strict limits were placed on groundwater pumping and the city switched to piped water from rivers, the sinking almost stopped. The lesson is that, unlike sea level rise, subsidence is largely a local problem with local solutions.

questions.text: Fermentation is one of the oldest food technologies we have. Long before anyone understood microbes, people discovered that leaving certain foods under the right conditions made them last longer and taste different. Bread, cheese, yoghurt, soy sauce and kimchi all depend on bacteria or yeasts transforming sugars into acids, gases or alcohol. The finished products are more acidic or salty than the raw ingredients, which stops harmful organisms from growing. In recent years, fermented foods have attracted attention for another reason: their possible effect on the gut. Some small trials suggest that eating them regularly increases the diversity of gut bacteria and reduces markers of inflammation. However, the evidence is still limited, and it is worth remembering that many shop-bought products are pasteurised, which kills the living cultures that may provide the benefit.

questions.text: We often talk about data travelling through the cloud, but almost all international internet traffic actually travels through cables on the sea floor. There are more than four hundred of them, some stretching over twenty thousand kilometres. Each is only about the thickness of a garden hose, with glass fibres carrying signals as pulses of light. Satellites carry a surprisingly small share of traffic, because cables are far cheaper per unit of data and much faster. The main threat to these cables is not sabotage but accidents: ships’ anchors and fishing trawlers cause most of the roughly one hundred and fifty faults each year. Repairs are handled by a small fleet of specialised ships, and because so many countries depend on a few routes, a single break can slow the internet for an entire region.

questions.text: One of the most striking findings in behavioural economics concerns organ donation. In some European countries, fewer than twenty per cent of people are registered donors, while in neighbouring countries with similar cultures the figure is above ninety per cent. The difference is not attitudes but defaults. Where people must opt in to become donors, most never get round to it. Where they are donors unless they opt out, most never opt out. Defaults work because they require no effort, and because people often interpret them as a recommendation. However, higher registration does not automatically mean more transplants, since families are usually consulted and hospitals need the capacity to act. So defaults are a powerful tool, but only one part of a system that has to work as a whole.

questions.text: Ask most people why ice is slippery and they will tell you that pressure from your shoe melts a thin film of water. That explanation has been in textbooks for a century, and it is wrong. The pressure a skater exerts lowers the melting point by a fraction of a degree, nowhere near enough to explain skating at minus twenty. What physicists now think is that the surface of ice is simply not solid in the way the inside is. The topmost molecules have neighbours only on one side, so they vibrate loosely and behave like a liquid even at low temperatures. This pre-melted layer is a few molecules thick and it exists whether you stand on it or not. Friction then adds a second effect: rubbing warms the surface and thickens the layer, which is why ice gets more slippery once you are moving. It also explains why ice below about minus forty is not slippery at all.

pressure lowers the melting point only a fraction of a degree
the surface of ice is pre-melted: loosely bound molecules behave like liquid
friction warms the surface and thickens that layer once you move
below about minus forty, ice is not slippery
questions.model: The lecturer argued that the familiar explanation of slippery ice, that pressure melts it, is wrong, because the pressure of a skate lowers the melting point by only a fraction of a degree. Instead, the surface molecules of ice have neighbours on one side only, so they behave like a liquid even when cold. Friction thickens this pre-melted layer once you move, and below about minus forty, ice is not slippery at all.

questions.text: The layout of a supermarket is not an accident, and almost none of it is designed for your convenience. Milk and bread, which most shoppers come for, sit at the very back, so you walk past everything else twice. The entrance is usually given to flowers and fruit, because colour and smell put people in a generous mood and, crucially, because buying something healthy first makes shoppers more willing to buy something indulgent later. Expensive brands are placed at eye level, with cheaper ones low down, and the sweets at the till catch tired children and tired adults alike. The aisles are wide enough for two trolleys because shoppers who are bumped from behind stop browsing. None of this is secret, and the research behind it is published. What is striking is how little the knowledge protects us: in studies, shoppers told in advance about these techniques spend just as much as shoppers who are not.

staples like milk are at the back, so you pass everything twice
fruit and flowers at the entrance improve mood and licence later treats
expensive brands sit at eye level; sweets wait at the till
knowing about the techniques does not reduce what shoppers spend
questions.model: The lecturer explained that supermarket layouts are designed to increase spending rather than to help shoppers. Expensive brands sit at eye level and sweets wait at the till. Strikingly, shoppers warned about these methods spend just as much.

questions.text: When the potato arrived in Europe from the Andes in the sixteenth century, nobody wanted it. It was not mentioned in the Bible, it grew underground, and it belonged to the same family as deadly nightshade, so it was widely believed to cause leprosy. Governments spent two centuries persuading people to eat it. A French pharmacist posted armed guards around a field of potatoes by day and withdrew them at night, correctly assuming that anything worth guarding was worth stealing. What finally changed minds was arithmetic. A field of potatoes feeds roughly three times as many people as the same field of wheat, and the crop survives weather and even armies, because it sits underground. By 1800 the potato underpinned the diet of northern Europe, and populations grew accordingly. The dependence also created the conditions for catastrophe: when a single disease reached Ireland in the 1840s, a country that had come to rely on one crop lost a quarter of its people.
keys: Europeans resisted the potato for two centuries
it was feared because it grew underground and resembled nightshade
officials used tricks, such as guarding a field to make it look valuable
the real argument was yield: about three times the people fed per field
dependence on one crop made the Irish famine catastrophic

questions.text: The Sahel is the belt of dry grassland that runs across Africa below the Sahara, and for decades the story told about it was simple: the desert was marching south, and a wall of trees would stop it. The Great Green Wall, launched in 2007, was planned as a line of forest eight thousand kilometres long. Twenty years on, less than a fifth of it exists, and the project has quietly changed shape, for good reasons. Satellite data showed that the Sahara is not advancing steadily; the boundary moves back and forth with rainfall, and much of the degradation is local, caused by overgrazing and the loss of tree cover on farmland rather than by sand arriving from the north. Planted seedlings in a line mostly died, because nobody owned them. What has worked is cheaper and less visible: farmers protecting the shoots that regrow naturally on their own fields. In Niger alone this has returned trees to some five million hectares.
keys: the Great Green Wall planned 8,000 km of trees across the Sahel
less than a fifth exists twenty years on
satellites showed the desert is not advancing steadily
degradation is mostly local: overgrazing and lost tree cover on farmland
farmer-managed natural regrowth worked better, about five million hectares in Niger

Protecting natural regrowth on farms has worked far better, restoring about five million hectares in Niger.

questions.text: If you watch a busy pavement from above, you see something that looks organised but nobody organises. Within about thirty seconds, two opposing streams of pedestrians sort themselves into lanes, and those lanes persist as long as the flow does. No one agrees to it; each walker is following two simple rules, roughly: move towards your goal, and avoid colliding. Models that give simulated pedestrians only those rules reproduce the lanes almost exactly, which is why the same models are used to design stations and stadiums. The interesting cases are where self-organisation fails. At a doorway, two streams trying to cross produce a blockage rather than lanes, and the standard fix is counter-intuitive: a pillar placed slightly off-centre in front of the door increases the flow, because it forces the crowd to form two stable streams instead of one contested one. The same principle explains why a wider exit is not always a faster one.

nobody coordinates it: walkers follow goal-seeking and collision-avoiding rules
simple models reproduce the behaviour and are used to design stations
self-organisation fails at doorways, where streams block each other
an off-centre pillar in front of a door increases flow

questions.text: A river running across a flat plain never stays straight, and the reason is not an obstacle. Start with a perfectly straight channel and a slight irregularity in the bank: the water on the outside of that small bend travels faster, so it cuts into the bank, while the slower water on the inside drops the sand it is carrying. The bend therefore grows, and grows faster the larger it becomes. What stops this from continuing forever is geometry. When a loop becomes so exaggerated that its two ends almost touch, the next flood cuts straight across the neck, abandoning the loop as a crescent-shaped lake, and the river is briefly straight again. Measure enough rivers and a constant appears: the distance along the channel is about three times the straight-line distance, on the Amazon and on a stream in a field alike. The pattern is so reliable that it has been used to identify river channels on Mars.
keys: rivers meander without any obstacle to deflect them
faster water erodes the outside of a bend, slower water deposits inside
bends therefore grow, and grow faster as they enlarge
a flood eventually cuts the neck, leaving an oxbow lake
channel length is about three times the straight-line distance, at any scale

Eventually a flood cuts across the neck, leaving an oxbow lake. Channel length is consistently about three times the straight-line distance, at every scale.

zh.The lecturer explained that rivers meand: 講者說明河流即使沒有障礙物也會蜿蜒。微小的不規則會使彎道外側的水流加快而侵蝕河岸，內側較慢的水流則堆積泥沙，於是彎道不斷擴大，而且越大擴張得越快。最後洪水會截穿曲頸，留下牛軛湖。河道長度一致地約為直線距離的三倍，在任何尺度上都成立。
zh.A river running across a flat plain neve: 流經平原的河流從來不會保持筆直，原因並不是遇到障礙物。假設一開始是一條完全筆直的河道，河岸上只有一點點不規則：那個小彎外側的水流速度較快，於是侵蝕河岸，而內側較慢的水流則把攜帶的沙子沉積下來。因此彎道會擴大，而且越大就擴張得越快。阻止這個過程無限持續下去的是幾何。當一個河曲誇張到兩端幾乎相接時，下一次洪水就會直接截穿這段窄頸，把河曲拋下成為一座新月形的湖泊，河流也短暫地恢復筆直。測量夠多的河流，就會出現一個常數：沿河道的距離大約是直線距離的三倍，亞馬遜河如此，田野間的小溪也是如此。這個規律非常可靠，甚至被用來辨認火星上的古河道。

questions.text: Lifespan across the animal kingdom varies by a factor of a thousand, and body size explains only part of it. A mouse lives three years and an elephant sixty, which fits the old idea that small animals burn energy faster and wear out sooner. But a bat is the size of a mouse and lives thirty years, and a naked mole rat lives past thirty with almost no cancer. What these long-lived exceptions share is protection from being eaten: bats fly, mole rats live underground, and both evolved under little pressure to breed early. Where predation is high, natural selection favours animals that reproduce quickly, and it stops caring what happens to the body afterwards, because few individuals live long enough for it to matter. Where predation is low, selection has time to favour better repair. That is why the same mouse, bred for generations on an island without predators, begins to live measurably longer.

bats and naked mole rats live far longer than their size predicts
what they share is protection from predators
high predation favours fast breeding and lets bodies decay
with low predation, selection favours better repair and longer life

questions.title: Should first-year exams be abolished?

turns.text: I think first-year exams should go. The first year is about adjusting to university, and high-stakes exams just push students into cramming. Continuous assessment — short essays, lab reports, quizzes — gives a far better picture of what someone can actually do.

The trouble with continuous assessment is that it’s much easier to get help with. An essay can be polished by a friend, or these days by software. An exam is the one situation where we know the work is the student’s own.

Both of those are true, but you’re treating it as all or nothing. The research on first-year retention suggests students drop out when they fail something big early and feel they don’t belong. The problem isn’t exams as such, it’s one exam deciding everything.
So you’d keep exams but lower the weight?
Exactly. Keep a supervised exam for integrity, but make it worth, say, thirty per cent, and let the rest come from work spread across the year.
I could live with that, as long as the exam still has to be passed on its own. Otherwise people will ignore it completely.

Grace: the real problem is one high-stakes exam; early failure drives dropout
proposal: keep a supervised exam worth about 30%, with the rest from coursework
Omar agrees, provided the exam must be passed on its own

questions.title: Should the city centre be closed to cars?

turns.text: Our city centre is choked with traffic, and the air quality readings on the high street are the worst in the region. Cities like Oslo and Ghent closed their centres to private cars and footfall actually went up. I think we should do the same.

I run a shop there, so I’m wary. Those cities had excellent public transport before the ban. Here, the buses stop at seven in the evening. If you close the centre tomorrow, my older customers simply won’t come.

I think the sequence is what matters. The evidence from Ghent is that they redesigned the bus network first and phased the restrictions in over two years. Doing it the other way round is how you get a backlash.
Fair enough. So start with the buses and delivery hours, then close streets gradually?
And keep access for disabled drivers and deliveries in the mornings. With that, I would support it.
And we should measure footfall and air quality before and after, so the decision rests on local data, not just examples from abroad.

Chen: measure footfall and air quality before and after

questions.title: AI tools and university assignments

turns.text: I use AI tools to brainstorm before I start an essay. They’re good at suggesting angles I wouldn’t have thought of, and I still write every sentence myself. Banning them feels like banning calculators.

The calculator comparison doesn’t really work, though. A calculator gives you a correct answer to a question you already understand. These tools can produce a plausible essay on a topic you don’t understand at all, and the marker can’t tell the difference.

I think we’re arguing about the wrong thing. Whether it’s allowed matters less than whether the assessment still measures learning. If an assignment can be completed entirely by a chatbot, the assignment is badly designed.
That’s convenient for students, but it puts the whole burden on lecturers to redesign everything overnight.
Not overnight. But more in-class writing, oral defences of essays, and asking students to show their drafts would all help.
And being honest about it. If each course said clearly what use is allowed, most students would follow the rules.

Aisha: the real question is whether assessment still measures learning; tasks a chatbot can complete are badly designed

solutions: in-class writing, oral defences and drafts, plus clear rules on allowed use (Ruby)

questions.title: A plant-based menu for the campus canteen?

turns.text: The sustainability committee wants the main canteen to go fully plant-based. Food is about a quarter of our campus emissions, and beef alone accounts for most of that. It’s the single biggest change we could make quickly.
I agree on the emissions, but a full switch removes choice, and I suspect students would just buy burgers off campus instead. Then emissions don’t fall; they just move somewhere we can’t see them.
There’s decent evidence on how to avoid that. Universities that made plant-based dishes the default, cheaper and placed first, saw meat sales fall by about a third without banning anything.
A third is good, but it’s not the same as eliminating beef.
No, but you could remove beef specifically, since it has by far the highest footprint, and keep chicken and fish on the menu.
That I could support. Drop beef, make the plant-based option the cheaper default, and publish the emissions figures each term so we can see if it works.

keys: Noah: food is about a quarter of campus emissions, mostly from beef; wants a fully plant-based canteen
Isabel: a full switch removes choice; students may eat off campus, so emissions just move
Kwame: making plant-based dishes the cheaper default cut meat sales by about a third
compromise: remove beef, but keep chicken and fish
plant-based as the cheaper default, with emissions published each term (Isabel)
questions.model: The speakers discussed making the campus canteen plant-based. Noah explained that food produces about a quarter of campus emissions, mostly from beef, and supported a full switch. Isabel agreed about emissions but warned that removing choice could push students to eat off campus, simply moving emissions elsewhere. Kwame cited evidence that making plant-based meals the cheaper default reduced meat sales by a third without bans. They reached a compromise: remove beef, keep chicken and fish, make plant-based dishes the default and publish emissions figures each term.

questions.title: Should the library open 24 hours?

turns.text: I think the library should stay open all night during exam periods. Lots of students work part-time or care for family during the day, and the evening is the only quiet time they get. Right now it closes at ten, just when some of us are getting started.
I understand that, but staffing a building all night is expensive, and the university says the money would come out of the book budget. I’d rather have the resources than the extra hours.

There’s also a wellbeing question. Some universities that tried twenty-four-hour opening found that a small group of students were basically living there and not sleeping. I’m not sure we want to encourage that.
That’s fair, but banning access doesn’t make people sleep. They just work somewhere worse.
What if only one floor stayed open overnight, with security rather than library staff? That would cost far less.
And limit it to the four weeks around exams. Then we could see how many people actually use it before deciding whether to make it permanent.

questions.title: Is a gap year worthwhile?

turns.text: I took a gap year before university and it was the best decision I made. I worked for six months, then volunteered abroad, and I arrived at university knowing what I wanted to study and why.

That worked for you, but a gap year assumes you can afford one. Travelling and volunteering abroad is expensive, and for many students the real choice is between starting their degree or starting work.

I think the useful part isn’t the travel at all. The research I’ve seen suggests students who take a year out do slightly better at university, but mainly because they’ve had time to mature and choose a course carefully.
That’s true — the six months of work taught me more than the volunteering, honestly.
Then universities could offer deferred places more easily, so that students can work locally for a year without losing their offer.
Exactly. A structured year of paid work, with the place held for you, gets the benefits without the cost.

questions.title: Should the city pay for a new stadium?

turns.text: I think the council should help fund the new stadium. It would bring major events to the city, create jobs during construction, and give the area around the old railway yard a reason to be regenerated.

The evidence on that is actually quite poor. Studies of publicly funded stadiums in many countries find little lasting economic benefit. Most of the spending on match days is money local people would have spent in the city anyway, just on something else.
I agree the economic case is weak, but I don’t think that’s the only question. A stadium can also matter for civic identity. The issue is who takes the risk if it loses money.
So you’d support it if the club carried the risk?
Largely, yes. The council could provide the land and transport links, which benefit everyone, while the club pays for the building itself.
I could accept that, as long as the council doesn’t guarantee the club’s loans. That’s where cities usually get burned.

Liam: stadiums matter for civic identity, but the key question is who carries the risk
proposal: the council provides land and transport, the club pays for the building
Priyanka agrees if the council does not guarantee the club’s loans

questions.title: Should restaurants add a service charge?

turns.text: I’d like restaurants to add a fixed service charge instead of relying on tips. Tipping makes staff income unpredictable, and research shows tips depend more on the customer’s mood and the server’s appearance than on the quality of service.
But a fixed charge removes the customer’s choice. If the service is poor, a tip is the only way I can show it. And some restaurants keep part of the service charge rather than passing it to staff.
In my country there’s no tipping at all — prices simply include fair wages. Service is excellent, because staff are trained and paid properly, not because they’re chasing tips.
So maybe the real solution isn’t a service charge but higher wages built into the menu prices.
I could accept that, if menu prices are clear and there’s no extra charge added at the end. What annoys people is surprises on the bill.
And any service charge that remains should go to staff by law, so customers know where their money is going.

questions.title: Should social media be restricted for under-16s?

turns.text: I support a legal minimum age of sixteen for social media. Rates of anxiety among teenagers have risen sharply since smartphones became common, and the platforms are designed to keep young people scrolling.

The timing is suggestive, but the research linking social media to teenage anxiety is actually quite mixed. Most studies find small average effects. And for some young people, especially those who feel isolated, online communities are a real lifeline.

I think we’re focusing on the wrong thing. A ban is almost impossible to enforce without checking everyone’s identity online. The design features are the problem — endless feeds, notifications at night, recommendation systems.
So you’d regulate the design rather than the age?
Yes. For example, no notifications overnight and no endless scrolling for younger users.
I’d support that, as long as young people can still reach support groups. And schools should teach how these platforms are designed to capture attention.

questions.title: Group projects: one mark or individual marks?

turns.text: I think group projects should give everyone the same mark. The whole point is learning to work as a team, and if marks are individual, people stop helping each other and just protect their own section.
But that’s exactly why shared marks feel unfair. In my last project, one person did almost nothing and got the same grade as the rest of us. It punishes the students who carry the work.
Some courses use peer assessment to deal with that. Each member rates the others’ contribution, and the group mark is adjusted up or down for each person.
Doesn’t that just turn into people voting for their friends?
It can, which is why the ratings need to be backed up by evidence, like meeting notes and a record of who did which task.
That would work for me. Keep one group mark, but let it be adjusted when there’s clear evidence that someone didn’t contribute.

questions.title: Should the campus ban plastic water bottles?

turns.text: I’d like the campus shops to stop selling bottled water altogether. Thousands of plastic bottles are thrown away here every week, and most of them are never recycled.

The problem is that some universities that banned bottled water saw sales of sugary drinks in plastic bottles go up. People still wanted something to drink on the go, so the plastic didn’t disappear, it just changed shape.

That’s the key point, I think. A ban only works if there’s a convenient alternative. At the moment there are only three water fountains on the whole campus, and one of them has been broken since September.
So we fix the fountains first?
Fix them and add refill stations in every building, and maybe give new students a free reusable bottle at enrolment.
Then phase out bottled water once the stations are in place, and track sales of other bottled drinks, so we know the plastic is actually going down.

questions.title: Should attendance at lectures be compulsory?

turns.text: I'd make attendance compulsory. Half my cohort has not been in a lecture theatre since October, and the ones who stop coming are the ones whose marks fall.

That gets the direction of causation backwards. Students stop coming because they are struggling, or working two jobs, not the other way round. Registers would punish the people who already have the least room to manoeuvre.

There is also the question of what they are missing. If a recorded lecture is as good as the live one, compulsory attendance is just theatre. If it isn't, we should ask why the live one adds so little.
It adds the chance to ask a question, and the fact that you are among people doing the same thing. That is hard to measure and easy to lose.
Then make it worth attending rather than mandatory. Our best-attended module has no register at all; it just has problem-solving in the room.
So the proposal is: no registers, keep the recordings, and move the activities that only work in person into the live session. And flag students who disappear for support rather than for a penalty.

questions.title: Should the campus charge for parking?

turns.text: Free parking sounds generous, but it is a subsidy to whoever drives, paid for by everyone. The land under that car park would take two hundred bed spaces.
Charge for it and you hit the cleaners and the night staff, who have no bus at six in the morning. The academics who can work from home will simply stop coming in.
Then price it by need rather than by status. Free for shift workers and blue-badge holders, charged for everyone else, and the money goes to the bus service.
That only works if the bus improves first. Charge in September and improve the buses in March and you will lose the argument permanently, whatever the policy's merits.
Sequencing I can accept. Buses first, then a charge, and the revenue ring-fenced so people can see where it goes.
And publish the numbers each year. If the charge does not cut traffic, we should say so rather than quietly keeping the income.

questions.title: Oral exams instead of final essays?

turns.text: I would replace the final essay with a twenty-minute oral. You cannot outsource a conversation, and in ten minutes I can tell whether someone understands their own argument.
You can also tell who is confident in a second language, which is not the same thing. My best student writes beautifully and freezes when questioned.
There is a workload point too. Three hundred students at twenty minutes each is a hundred hours of staff time, before marking or moderation.
Fewer hours than marking three hundred essays properly, in my experience. And the feedback is immediate, which the essay never is.
Then use it as a check rather than a replacement. Keep the essay, and call a sample of students in to discuss what they wrote.
A sample is defensible if it is random and everyone knows it could be them. Record the sessions, so a disputed mark can be reviewed by someone else.

zh.Leo: Then use it as a check rather than: Leo: 那就把它當成查核，而不是取代。保留報告，再找一部分學生來談談他們寫了什麼。
zh.Hana: A sample is defensible if it is ra: Hana: 只要抽樣是隨機的，而且大家都知道自己可能被抽到，這就站得住腳。過程要錄影，萬一分數有爭議，可以讓別人複核。

questions.title: A new gym or more scholarships?

turns.text: We have one unexpected donation and two proposals: a sports building, or forty more bursaries a year for a decade. I would take the bursaries without hesitation.
Bursaries help forty people. The building helps everybody for forty years, and it is the sort of thing nobody will ever fund later, because maintenance is unglamorous.
That cuts the other way, Tom. A building commits us to heating and repairing it for decades out of money we do not yet have. A bursary ends cleanly.
And we know what bursaries do. The students who get them finish their degrees at the same rate as everyone else; without them, a third drop out.
I would still argue for something physical, but I accept the running costs point. Perhaps refurbish the sports hall we have rather than build a new one.
That I could support: a modest refurbishment now, the remainder to bursaries, and a rule that no new building is approved without its maintenance funded.

keys: Amara prefers forty bursaries a year to a new sports building
Tom argues a building serves everyone for decades and will never be funded later
Rachel warns a building commits the university to decades of running costs
Amara cites evidence that bursary students complete at normal rates
agreed: refurbish the existing hall, spend the rest on bursaries, fund maintenance before approving buildings
questions.model: The group debated whether a donation should fund a sports building or bursaries. Amara preferred forty bursaries a year, citing evidence that recipients complete their degrees at normal rates. Tom argued a building serves everyone for decades and would never attract funding later, while Rachel warned that it commits the university to decades of heating and repairs. They settled on refurbishing the existing hall, spending the remainder on bursaries, and funding maintenance before approving any new building.

zh.Amara prefers forty bursaries a year to: Amara 偏好每年四十個助學金，而不是新的運動館
zh.Tom argues a building serves everyone fo: Tom 主張建築能服務所有人數十年，日後也不會有人願意出資

zh.Tom: Bursaries help forty people. The bu: Tom: 助學金幫到四十個人。建築則在四十年間幫到所有人，而且這種東西以後不會有人願意出錢，因為維護一點都不光鮮。
zh.Rachel: That cuts the other way, Tom. A: Rachel: Tom，這個論點也可以反過來說。一棟建築會讓我們用還沒到手的錢，承擔數十年的暖氣和維修。助學金則是乾淨地結束。
zh.Amara: And we know what bursaries do. Th: Amara: 而且我們很清楚助學金的效果。領到的學生完成學業的比率和其他人一樣；沒有助學金，他們有三分之一會中途退學。
zh.Tom: I would still argue for something p: Tom: 我還是主張要有實體的東西，但我接受營運成本這個論點。或許整修現有的體育館，而不是新蓋一棟。
zh.Rachel: That I could support: a modest r: Rachel: 這我可以支持：現在做適度整修，其餘用於助學金，並訂下一條規則——任何新建築在維護經費到位之前都不得核准。

questions.title: Should employers still ask for exam grades?

turns.text: We are still asking applicants for grades they earned at sixteen. For a thirty-year-old with eight years of work behind them, that tells us nothing useful.
It tells us something about consistency when there is nothing else to go on. For a graduate with no work history, grades are the only evidence we have.
Then use them only in that case. The way we do it now, the filter runs on everyone, and it screens out people who went back to study at twenty-five and did well.

There is a measurable cost as well. Our own data shows no relationship between school grades and performance reviews after the first year. We are filtering on something we have already shown does not predict.
If the data says that, I am not going to defend the filter. But I want a replacement, not just its removal — otherwise we are back to who interviews well.
A short work sample marked blind would do it, and we already use one for the technical roles. Grades for recent school leavers only, work sample for everyone else.

keys: Nadia objects to asking experienced applicants for grades earned at sixteen
Victor says grades are the only evidence for candidates with no work history
Nadia replies the filter runs on everyone and screens out late returners
Chen cites company data showing no link between grades and later performance
agreed: grades only for recent school leavers, a blind work sample for everyone else
questions.model: The group discussed whether employers should keep asking for school grades. Nadia objected that experienced applicants are still filtered on results earned at sixteen, which screens out people who returned to study later. zh.The group discussed whether employers sh: 小組討論雇主是否還應該要求提供在學成績。Nadia 反對讓有經驗的求職者仍以十六歲的成績被篩選，認為這會刷掉較晚重返校園的人。Victor 回應，對沒有工作經歷的人而言，成績是唯一的依據。Chen 則引用公司資料，指出成績與第一年之後的考績毫無關聯。他們最後同意：成績只用於剛離校的求職者，其餘人一律採用匿名評分的工作樣本。
zh.Nadia: We are still asking applicants fo: Nadia: 我們到現在還在要求應徵者提供他們十六歲時考到的成績。對一個已經工作八年的三十歲求職者來說，那根本說明不了什麼。
zh.Victor: It tells us something about cons: Victor: 在沒有其他依據時，它多少說明了一個人的穩定表現。對沒有工作經歷的畢業生而言，成績是我們唯一握有的證據。
Nadia: 那就只在那種情況下使用。我們現在的做法是讓這道篩選套用在所有人身上，結果刷掉了二十五歲才回去唸書、而且表現很好的人。
zh.Chen: There is a measurable cost as well: Chen: 這還有可以量化的代價。我們自己的資料顯示，學校成績與第一年之後的考績毫無關聯。我們是在用一個已經證明沒有預測力的東西來篩選。
zh.Victor: If the data says that, I am not: Victor: 如果資料是這樣，我不會替這道篩選辯護。但我要的是替代方案，而不只是把它拿掉——否則我們又回到誰面試表現好的老路。
zh.Chen: A short work sample marked blind w: Chen: 一份匿名評分的簡短工作樣本就可以，技術職我們本來就在用。成績只用於剛離校的人，其他人一律用工作樣本。

questions.title: Should the university fund the student paper?

turns.text: The paper is about to close. Advertising collapsed years ago, and the three of them are paying for printing out of their own pockets.
If the university funds it, the university owns it. The first time they investigate the vice-chancellor's expenses, someone will quietly review the grant.
That is an argument for how it is funded, not whether. A fixed three-year grant that nobody can vary mid-term removes most of the leverage.
Or fund it through the students' union, so the money arrives at one remove. Unions are not perfectly independent either, but they are not the subject of most of the reporting.
A grant through the union, fixed for three years, published in full — I could support that. What I will not support is an annual line item the press office can lean on.
Then write the editorial independence into the grant conditions, and give the editors the right to publish any attempt to interfere.

keys: Olivia says the student paper is closing as advertising has gone
Bilal warns that university funding brings university influence
Olivia argues the issue is how it is funded, suggesting a fixed three-year grant
Farah proposes routing the money through the students' union
agreed: a published three-year grant via the union, with editorial independence written in

They agreed on a published three-year grant via the union, with editorial independence written into its conditions.

zh.Olivia says the student paper is closing: Olivia 指出學生報因廣告收入消失而即將停刊
zh.Bilal warns that university funding brin: Bilal 警告由校方出資就會帶來校方的影響力

zh.Bilal: A grant through the union, fixed: Bilal: 透過學生會、鎖定三年、全額公開的補助——這我可以支持。我不能接受的是每年編列、新聞室隨時可以施壓的一筆預算。
zh.Farah: Then write the editorial independ: Farah: 那就把編輯獨立寫進補助條件，並賦予編輯權利，把任何干預的企圖公諸於世。

questions.title: Should the department cut staff flights?

turns.text: Flights are two-thirds of the department's emissions. Everything else we have done — the solar panels, the recycling — is a rounding error next to the conference travel.
And conferences are how early-career researchers get known. Senior staff already have their networks; a cut would fall hardest on the people who need the room most.
Then protect their travel explicitly and cut ours. A budget of one long-haul trip every two years for anyone with a permanent post would halve the total.
Rail should also count differently. Paris and Berlin are overnight trains, but the booking system will not price a sleeper against a flight, so everyone flies by default.
Fix the booking system first, then. Half of this is not principle, it is that the easy option happens to be the worst one.
So: rail quoted first for anything under ten hours, a flight budget that protects early-career staff, and the department publishes its emissions each year.

keys: Gabriel says flights are two-thirds of departmental emissions
Mei warns cuts would fall hardest on early-career researchers who need conferences
Gabriel proposes protecting their travel and limiting permanent staff to one long-haul trip every two years
Ana notes the booking system never offers rail, so flying is the default
agreed: rail quoted first under ten hours, a protected budget, emissions published annually

They agreed to quote rail first for journeys under ten hours, protect early-career budgets and publish emissions annually.

zh.Gabriel: Flights are two-thirds of the d: Gabriel: 搭飛機佔了系上排放量的三分之二。我們做的其他事——太陽能板、回收——跟會議差旅相比都只是零頭。
zh.Mei: And conferences are how early-caree: Mei: 可是研討會正是年輕研究者打開知名度的方式。資深同仁早就有自己的人脈；刪減會對最需要那個場合的人衝擊最大。
zh.Gabriel: Then protect their travel expli: Gabriel: 那就明確保障他們的差旅，刪我們自己的。凡是有專任職位的人，每兩年只能有一趟長程，這樣總量就能減半。
Ana: 鐵路也應該用不同的方式計算。到巴黎和柏林都有夜車，但訂票系統不會把臥鋪和機票放在一起比價，結果大家預設都搭飛機。
Mei: 那就先修訂票系統。這件事有一半不是原則問題，而是最省事的選項剛好是最糟的選項。
zh.Ana: So: rail quoted first for anything: Ana: 所以：十小時以內的行程優先報價鐵路、機票額度要保障年輕研究者，而且系上每年公布自己的排放量。

questions.text: Your neighbour has been playing loud music late every night this week, and you have an important exam tomorrow morning. You knock on their door. What do you say?
keys: greet politely and introduce yourself
describe the problem specifically: loud music late at night
explain why it matters now: tomorrow’s exam
make a clear, reasonable request
keep the tone friendly so the relationship stays positive
questions.model: Hi, sorry to bother you — I’m Alex from the flat next door. I wanted to have a quick word about the music in the evenings. This week it has been quite loud after eleven, and it comes straight through my bedroom wall. Normally I wouldn’t mind, but I have an important exam at nine tomorrow morning and I really need a good night’s sleep. Would you mind keeping it down after about ten tonight? And if you’re planning a party at the weekend, just let me know and I’ll make other plans. Thanks so much, I really appreciate it.

zh.Your neighbour has been playing loud mus: 這一週你的鄰居每天深夜都大聲放音樂，而你明天早上有一場重要的考試。你去敲他們的門。你會怎麼說？

zh.describe the problem specifically: loud: 具體描述問題：深夜音樂太大聲
zh.explain why it matters now: tomorrow’s e: 說明為什麼現在這件事很重要：明天的考試
zh.make a clear, reasonable request: 提出清楚且合理的請求
zh.keep the tone friendly so the relationsh: 保持友善的語氣，讓鄰居關係維持良好
zh.Hi, sorry to bother you — I’m Alex from: 嗨，不好意思打擾你——我是住隔壁的 Alex。我想跟你稍微談一下晚上音樂的事。這一週十一點以後音樂都滿大聲的，聲音直接穿過我臥室的牆。平常我不會介意，但我明天早上九點有一場重要的考試，真的需要好好睡一覺。今晚大概十點以後，可以請你把音量調小一點嗎？如果你週末打算辦派對，跟我說一聲就好，我會另外安排。非常謝謝你，真的很感激。

questions.text: You are a team leader at work. A colleague who is usually reliable has missed two deadlines this month. You meet him privately to discuss it. What do you say?
keys: open supportively and state the purpose of the meeting
describe the facts, the two missed deadlines, without blaming
ask whether something is affecting his work
agree practical next steps or support
confirm what is expected for the next deadline
questions.model: Thanks for making time, Sam. I wanted to talk privately because you are normally one of the most reliable people on the team, and this month two deadlines have slipped — the client report and the budget summary. I’m not here to criticise; I’d just like to understand what’s going on. Is something making the workload difficult at the moment, either at work or outside it? If it’s a matter of too many projects, we can look at moving one to someone else. What I do need is for the next report to be ready by the fifteenth, so let’s agree now what would make that realistic.

zh.open supportively and state the purpose: 以支持的態度開場，並說明這次談話的目的
zh.describe the facts, the two missed deadl: 陳述事實——錯過了兩次截止期限——而不帶責備
zh.ask whether something is affecting his w: 詢問是否有什麼事情影響了他的工作
zh.agree practical next steps or support: 商定實際可行的下一步或支援方式
zh.confirm what is expected for the next de: 確認下一個截止期限的要求
zh.Thanks for making time, Sam. I wanted to: Sam，謝謝你抽出時間。我想私下跟你談談，因為你平常是團隊裡最可靠的人之一，但這個月有兩個期限延誤了——客戶報告和預算摘要。我不是來批評你的，只是想了解發生了什麼事。目前是不是有什麼事情讓工作量變得吃力，不管是工作上還是工作以外的？如果是專案太多的問題，我們可以考慮把其中一個轉給別人。我確實需要下一份報告在十五號之前完成，所以我們現在就來談談，怎麼做才能讓這個目標實際可行。

questions.text: You ordered a laptop online, but it arrived with a cracked screen. You call the company’s customer service line. What do you say?
keys: identify yourself and the order clearly
describe the damage precisely
say when it arrived and that it was damaged on delivery

ask about the next steps and how long they will take

When I opened the box, the screen was cracked across the bottom left corner, so it must have been damaged before it reached me — the packaging was dented as well. I have taken photos of both the screen and the box. I would like a replacement sent out as soon as possible, or a full refund if that model is out of stock. Could you tell me how to return the damaged one and how long the replacement will take?

zh.You ordered a laptop online, but it arri: 你在網路上訂購了一台筆記型電腦，但送到時螢幕是裂的。你打電話給這家公司的客服專線。你會怎麼說？

zh.state the outcome you want: a replacemen: 表明你希望的處理方式：換貨或退款
zh.ask about the next steps and how long th: 詢問接下來的步驟以及需要多久時間
zh.Hello, I’m calling about an order I rece: 你好，我打來是想詢問我昨天收到的一筆訂單。訂單編號是 48213，是一台十四吋的筆記型電腦。我打開箱子時，螢幕左下角有一道裂痕，所以一定是在送到我手上之前就已經損壞了——包裝也有凹痕。我已經把螢幕和箱子都拍了照片。我希望你們盡快寄一台新的給我，如果那個型號缺貨，就請全額退款。可以請你告訴我要怎麼退回損壞的那台，以及換貨需要多久時間嗎？
